listings.name: Prague Visitor Pass
listings.content: The official city pass providing free public transport, a free ticket to ride on the vintage tram line 42 as well as free entry to various city attractions.

listings.name: Prague Cool Pass
listings.content: An unofficial pass available for 1, 2 or 3 days. Includes a bus city tour and a river cruise. Free entry to Prague Castle – St.Vitus Cathedral, Royal Palace, Golden Lane, St.George's Basilica. Free entry to Jewish Museum – synagogues and famous Old Jewish Cemetery (6 sites). In total, free entry to 50 attractions and discounts on over 30 attractions. Free guidebook with information about the attractions in 7 languages.

listings.name: Prague City Pass
listings.content: An unofficial pass providing free entry to various attractions in Prague within a 30 days period, various 25% discounts, sightseeing tours. Prague Castle – Old Royal Palace with Vladislav Hall, St. George‘s Basilica, Golden Lane with Daliborka Tower, St. Vitus Cathedral. The ticket is valid for 2 days from first entry. Jewish Museum in Prague – Maisel Synagogue, Spanish Synagogue, Pinkas Synagogue, Old Jewish Cemetery, Klausen Synagogue, Ceremonial Hall. The ticket is valid for 7 days from first entry.

listings.name: National Gallery Gift Ticket
listings.content: If you are an art lover and you are staying in Prague for a longer time, a dárková vstupenka (gift ticket) for National Gallery may save you money. The ticket is valid for a year and is valid in all exhibitions (both permanent and non-permanent) of National Gallery. Number of visits is not limited. A gift ticket for one person costs 650 Kč, for two persons 1000 Kč. For 240 Kč you can have one-person ticket valid for two days in all "Old Art" exhibitions of National Gallery (Šternberk Palace, Schwarzenberg Palace, St. Anežka Convent), basic entry for these three galleries bought separately would cost you.

listings.name: Prague Spring
listings.content: The most famous classical music festival in the Czech republic.

listings.name: Signal Festival
listings.content: A weekend in October, during which many historic buildings are lighted by spectacular video-mappings and many light-and-sound installations are set up at different places in the city centre, Vinohrady and Karlín.

listings.name: Wine Boat
listings.content: The 1-hour cruise includes a visit of Prague Venice river canal as well as wine tasting of local wines.

listings.name: Prague Steam Boats
listings.content: Offer one hour cruises, as well as cruises to the Zoo and full day cruises to Slapy water dam. If you have the time for a 3-hour dinner cruise, you will certainly enjoy viewing the city from the river, while savouring a great dinner.

listings.name: Cruise Prague
listings.content: Offers a wide range of regular and private cruises.

listings.name: JazzBoat
listings.content: Combines cruising and jazz concerts.

listings.name: Football
listings.content: The city's leading soccer team is SK Slavia Praha. They play in the First League, the top tier, and often qualify for European tournaments. They play at the 21,000 capacity Fortuna Arena, which is also the usual venue for international matches; it's 5 km southeast of the old city centre. The city's other First League sides are AC Sparta Prague (at Generali Arena, 1 km north of the centre) and Bohemians at Ďolíček stadium in Vršovice district. FK Dukla Prague (at Stadion Juliska in the northern suburb of Dejvice) play in the National League, the second tier.

listings.name: We Bike Prague
listings.content: With We Bike Prague team you can easily discover the city of Prague and the area around. Very good quality bike to rent for you self guided trip in the city and multidays trip through the countryside. We Bike Prague is also specialized in long distance bike trip. Good bikes, panniers and maps can be rented for your cycling holiday in the Czech Republic.

listings.name: BIKO Adventures Prague
listings.content: BIKO offers mountain bike, road bike and outdoor activities off the beaten track in Prague and in the Czech Republic. From easy to advanced. High end bike rental: touring bikes, hardtail and full suspension MTB, road bikes, e-MTB.

listings.name: Prague Tours Center
listings.content: A free offer for the visitors of Prague: the Prague Tours Centre is offering free connection and charge up of your electric bikes and Segway PT. While connected, the devices are guarded by a supervisor and, in the meantime, you can take walk around Prague, visit a museum or your preferred restaurant. In the Prague Tours Centre the tourists have a possibility of depositing their bikes together with baggage which they do not want to carry or leave in the streets. The Prague Tours Centre also offers facilities for washing your bike or borrowing a complete bike repair kit for free.

listings.name: Running Tours Prague
listings.content: Activity for those into running who want to explore the city and stay fit. It shows runners of all abilities around the city's musts while on the run. A traveling runner introduces the best of the Prague to their running shoes and feels just like a local runner. It usually takes 50–120 mins and 7–13. Your running in Prague is 100 percent customizable as to date, time, pace and distance.

listings.name: Prague Castle
listings.content: The former seat of the King and is now the seat of the Czech president. This is Prague's number one tourist attraction so expect huge crowds and possibly long lines, especially during high tourist season. Your best bet is to come early, as soon as the castle opens. Similar to other royal palaces, there is an hourly changing of the guard ceremony. At noon, the ceremony includes fanfare at a flag ceremony in the first courtyard.

listings.name: St. Vitus Cathedral
listings.content: In the center of the castle and the most important cathedral in all of the Czech republic. The oldest parts of the cathedral are from the 14th century, but the cathedral was not completed in the Medieval period. The highest tower was completed in Renaissance and Baroque styles much later, as is clearly obvious. The Western portal and both Western towers are even younger, completed in the 19th and early 20th centuries. However, the original Medieval plans were used for them and their relatively small age is not obvious. St. Vitus Cathedral was the place of royal coronations and also the location of the remains of several famous Czech Kings (notably Charles IV, of Charles Bridge fame). Go around the cathedral so you not only see the Western portal with the rose window and beautiful gargoyles, but also the original medieval Golden Portal in the south and the stunning Flying Buttresses in the east. Things not to miss inside the cathedral include the stained glass Rose Window in the west portal, the stained glass window by Alfons Mucha, the tomb of St. John of Nepomuk made of pure silver, the Royal Crypt underneath the cathedral (with the graves of Charles IV, his four wives, Wenceslas IV, Ladislas the Posthumous, George of Podebrady, Rudolf II, and Marie Amalie of Austria, the daughter of Maria Theresa of Austria) and the stunning St. Wenceslas Chapel with the relics of the saint and walls decorated with gold and more than 1300 gems. The Czech Coronation Jewels are kept behind the door with the seven locks (seven important people including the Czech President and the Czech Prime Minister keep the keys) in the St. Wenceslas Chapel. If you're willing to hike the 287 stairs to the top of the Bell Tower (the one with Baroque roof) you'll be rewarded with excellent views of the castle and the surrounding area. The Bell Tower holds Zikmund, the biggest bell in the Czech Republic.

listings.name: Old Royal Palace
listings.content: The original seat of Czech rulers. Visitors first enter the Vladislav hall, the largest high-Gothic vaulted space in Central Europe. Other rooms include the Palace chapel and throne room. At the end of the exhibit is "The Story of Prague Castle" exhibit, which features artificats from the castle's past. The Old Royal Palace is occasionally closed to visitors, so it may be advisable to check this before visiting.

listings.name: St. George's Basilica
listings.content: The second oldest church in the castle and features a colorful Baroque facade. The interior is visibly older and is the burial place of the Premyslid family and the first Czech saint, Princess Ludmila.

listings.name: St. George's Convent - National Gallery
listings.content: One of several branches of the National Gallery is located inside this, the first convent in Bohemia. Today it houses the collection of Czech Mannerist and Baroque art.

listings.name: The Golden Lane
listings.content: During the reign of Rudolf II, goldsmiths lived in a lively alleyway filled with tiny workshops, which were also their residence, hence its name. Tiny, cobblestoned walkway filled with brightly-painted little houses, where modern man has a hard time standing with the low ceiling. (It's tough to realize just how tiny our pre-20th-century ancestors were until you go somewhere like this). Franz Kafka occupied No. 22 from 1916 to 1917, and this is why most people visit the Golden Lane. There is also a Renaissance tavern, a castle guard's house including his colorful uniform, and a goldsmith's shop shown as they might have looked during the periods represented, and those are interesting. Otherwise, there really isn't another good reason unless you want to buy some overpriced souvenirs in the small shops now occupying the houses.

listings.name: The Daliborka
listings.content: Built by Prince Vladislav in 1496, the tower at the far end of the castle is part of a new fortified wall. Its first prisoner was a recalcitrant knight named Dalibor who, according to legend, played his violin very sadly at the wall serenading the castle residents. Though, the thickness of the walls makes that legend a little unlikely. No one would have been able to hear him outside! Today the tower holds a small display of prison and torture techniques used during that time.

listings.name: Prague Castle Picture Gallery
listings.content: Housed in the original castle stables. It contains Renaissance and Baroque art, including parts of the original collection of Rudolph II.

listings.name: The Royal Garden
listings.content: To the east/north-east of the palace is a large park. Aside from its own beauty, it has an excellent view of the east bank of the river. Entrance is free.

listings.name: The State Rooms at Prague Castle
listings.content: Open to the public two days of the year, as they are mostly used exclusively by the President. Contact the Castle Information office for more details.

listings.name: Charles Bridge
listings.content: connects the Old Town with Lesser Town. Commissioned by Czech king and Holy Roman Emperor Charles IV and constructed between 1357 and 1402, it is one of the most interesting historical stone bridges in Europe. It is 516 meters long with 16 arches. Baroque statues (a total of 30) began to be placed here in the 17th century. The best time to visit the bridge is in the quiet morning or in the evening at sunset, when one can enjoy a view of the fully lit Prague Castle.
listings.image: Prague 07-2016 View from Petrinska Tower img2.jpg

listings.name: The Lennon Wall
listings.content: This historic graffiti wall, near a Venetian-like canal with water wheel and close to the Charles Bridge, used to be a source of irritation to the communist regime. a wall in Prague, Czechia. After the 1980 murder of John Lennon, a mural of John Lennon was painted by an unknown artist. As more people expanded upon it, the wall became a place for free expression of then communist Czechoslovakia. It is now an open-air gallery, with restricted space for marking with pencils, markers, or chalk.

listings.name: Child Jesus of Prague
listings.content: This image of Christ, known also as the Holy Infant of Prague, is among the most widespread religious images in the world. The statue was brought from Spain in the 16th century and given to the Carmelites in 1628. It is 47 cm high and represents Jesus as a Child and King. The statue is carved out of wood and the surface is modeled in coloured wax. The entrance to the church is free of charge.

listings.name: Petřín Hill
listings.content: Due to a housing crunch, most young Czechs don't move out of their parents' house until they marry (sometimes long after!) This lack of privacy leads to some very public displays of affection – what you see on the metro or trams won't compare to what you’re likely to encounter on Petřín Hill. This hillside slopes down from the Castle and Strahov Monastery to Malá Strana and Malostranské náměstí metro station. It affords an amazing view of the city on a clear day, and in springtime the trees are all in bloom. This is possibly the nicest place to kick back with a bottle of wine and your significant other to watch the sun set over the city. Just be careful not to trip over the modesty-lacking couples who will probably already be there. In a city filled with apartment buildings and only a handful of single family houses (almost all in the diplomats' favoured housing area, Dejvice, and priced far above the average Czech family's wage) parks take on a greater importance. The most famous "inhabitant" of the park is a statue of poet Karel Hynek Mácha, at whose feet lovers leave wreaths every spring in honour of his romantic poem Máj.

listings.name: Petřín Lookout Tower
listings.content: A smaller version of the Eiffel Tower on the top of Petrin Hill overlooking Prague. The grounds near the tower contain a formal rose garden which is free to walk around. With a height of just under 60 m, it is about 1/5th scale of the Paris Eiffel tower, and was constructed shortly after its Parisian counterpart at the end of the 19th century. The tower has 2 viewing platforms, one about halfway, and one at the top. A complete ascent takes about 220 steps. Strong winds (which are common in Prague) make the tower wobble, which can be felt on the upper deck and can induce motion sickness in some visitors.
listings.price: Climbing the tower costs 220 Kč for a standard ticket or 150 Kč for discounts. Only ISIC cards are accepted for student discounts. Paid lift available (additional 150 Kč for adults) which takes you to the observation platform
listings.image: Prague 07-2016 View from Lesser Town Nicholas Church img5.jpg

listings.name: Loreta
listings.content: A beautiful Baroque convent in the Lesser Town.

listings.name: Strahov Monastery
listings.content: A monastery on the mountain. Worth a visit for both its picture gallery and its notable Renaissance library.

listings.name: Franz Kafka Museum
listings.content: Influences, life and works of the German language writer.

listings.name: Wallenstein Palace
listings.content: A nice Baroque palace with garden, it houses the Senate of the Czech Republic.

listings.name: The Pedagogical Comenius Museum
listings.content: A museum documenting the writings of the Czech Renaissance erudite, centering around the legacy of J.A. Comenius: traditions and challenges of the Czech culture and education. The story starts in the 9th century with early Christian literacy, detailing the role of Prague and its university in the European and international context. The Golden Age of humanism lays the foundations of modern pedagogy, with are explained to visitors with numerous displays and original artifacts. Plan enough time for your visit, because a complete tour takes at least 2 - 3 hours, and keeping in mind that the museum closes relatively early.

listings.name: Lobkowicz Palace
listings.content: Art museum near Prague Castle. Houses the original manuscript for Beethoven's famous 5th symphony, and many other interesting artifacts.

listings.name: Museum Kampa
listings.content: A museum of modern Central European art.
listings.price: Adults 350 Kč, student/senior 190 Kč, child (under 6) free

listings.name: National Gallery Prague - Old Masters
listings.content: The Old Masters collection of the National Gallery, covering paintings from the 15th to 18th centuries, is divided between two mansions on Hradčanské Square, the Renaissance Schwarzenberg Palace and the Baroque Sternberg Palace.
listings.price: Combined entrance to both buildings 300 Kč (reductions 200 Kč), also other combined passes with other NGP branches

listings.name: U krále Brabantského
listings.content: Tavern opened daily since 1375, recreating the ambient of 14th century Medieval Prague. Includes Medieval furniture and wall decorations, traditional food, and live entertainment by bards and sword fighters. Reservations recommended. An all-in evening package costs 1200 Kč.

listings.name: U Zavesenyho Kafe
listings.content: one of the very few restaurants in the tourist area of Prague with a quirky atmosphere that isn't excessively touristy. Offering food at reasonable prices and serving good, modest food. A great place to have lunch while exploring Hradčany and Petrin Park, it's conveniently located in the middle between these two tourist attractions.

listings.name: Restaurant U Zlatých nůžek
listings.content: offers a wide selection of Czech and international cuisine including first-class Moravian wines. Enjoy the unique atmosphere of calmness in the centre of Prague with its beautiful view of the Charles Bridge and enjoy the garden in front of the hotel during the summer season (May-October). The restaurant is suitable for family gatherings, company events and wedding celebrations.

listings.name: El Centro
listings.content: An excellent little restaurant located near the Charles Bridge, but tucked behind a couple of other buildings. It's a typical Spanish restaurant, has a very friendly atmosphere, good prices and isn't crowded. Also, it doesn't have any hidden charges such as service taxes which are common in Prague. English menus and takeout available.

listings.name: Malostranska Pivnice
listings.content: Traditional Czech cuisine. Sometimes you get a hand written bill with a service charge. Do not pay it. Tip only as much as you like.

listings.name: Červená Sedma
listings.content: Traditional food serving tourists, tables outside in pedestrian area.

listings.name: LoVeg
listings.content: Vegan restaurant serving local Czech dishes and international cuisine.

listings.name: St. Martin
listings.content: Cozy restaurant with Czech and American cuisine, next to the KGB Museum. Suitable for small groups or families with children. Reservations usually not necessary. Their home made ice tea is worth a visit.

listings.name: Kampa Park Restaurant
listings.content: High quality (and price) restaurant with excellent view of the Charles bridge and river.

listings.name: Střelecký ostrov
listings.content: Terrace provide a nice place to sit and drink and admire the view over the river.

listings.name: U Glaubiců
listings.content: Classic Czech pub, serving some of the best and cheapest beer in Malá Strana, normally one of the most expensive areas of the city.

listings.name: U Malého Glena
listings.content: American-owned bar with live jazz downstairs nightly. See video of this bar.

listings.name: Dobrá trafika
listings.content: Cosy cafe near Kampa with nice atmosphere, small garden and variety of small snacks and hot drinks. The cafe is located behind a newsstand (in Czech - trafika).

listings.name: Cafe Club Ujezd
listings.content: Kind of an odd bar in Mala Strana. Interesting art on the walls and ceilings. Even more interesting clientele. Cheap beer and a great place for groups.

listings.name: EA Hotel Jeleni dvur
listings.content: All 30 rooms are equipped with TV/SAT, high speed Internet connection, direct dial telephone and safe deposit box. Public PC desk with Internet access and printer is available at the reception. Some rooms offer a wonderful view of the historical parts of Prague. There is a parking lot in front of the hotel for those coming by car.

listings.name: Golden Well Hotel
listings.content: Boutique hotel with one of the most beautiful views in Prague and restaurant terrace leading directly to Prague Castle.

listings.name: Hotel Questenberk
listings.content: Romantic, baroque-style, 17th century hotel. Each of the Single, Double, Deluxe Double rooms and the three Royal apartments are originally furnished and equipped with TV, WiFi, phone, safe, and minibar.

listings.name: Arpacay Hostel
listings.content: Facilities include a kitchen, laundry and personal lockers. There's also a roof top terrace overlooking the city. Free breakfast, linens and internet access. There's no curfew.

listings.name: The Charles Hotel
listings.content: Josefska 1; Romantic 4-star hotel near to the Charles Bridge. Some rooms have antique wooden painted ceilings. Rooms are air-conditioned and equipped with safe, satellite tv, phone and minibar. Each room has private bathroom and free WiFi.

listings.name: Hotel Sax
listings.content: 4-star vintage design hotel. Every room or suite has an original appearance: design of the 1970s, furniture of the 1950s or 1960s.

listings.name: Nerudova Apartment House
listings.content: All apartments are fully furnished in standard way. A spacious living room includes a fully equipped kitchenette and a dinette. Maid service twice per week. Prices vary according to the season and type of apartment, from €50 for one bedroom apartment to €150 for large three bedroom apartment.

listings.name: Pension Dietzenhofer
listings.content: The main house is a cute green building dating from 1572. Rooms and suites there start from 1500 kc for a single. The flat, which sleeps up to 4, is a great value for backpackers at 1800 Kč/night. It has a fully equipped kitchen, dining room, bathroom, and is located on Karmelitska, a main thoroughfare in Lesser Town.

listings.name: Alchymist Grand Hotel and Spa
listings.content: Very luxurious, and rather expensive hotel located across the street from the U.S. Embassy.

listings.name: Mandarin Oriental Prague
listings.content: Part of the Mandarin Oriental chain. Very expensive.

listings.name: Best Western Hotel Kampa
listings.content: Authentically decorated hotel evokes the splendour of the 17th century and welcomes its guests with wonderful internal architecture and pleasant hotel comfort.

listings.name: Prague Residences
listings.content: Modern short term accommodation in fully serviced apartments.

listings.name: Wenceslas Square
listings.content: Václavské náměstí is a wide boulevard running down from the National Museum and it's crammed with bars, restaurants and casinos. It is the heart of central Prague. All three metro lines cross there: line A and C cross at "Muzeum" station (upper part of boulevard next to National Museum), while lines A and B cross at "Můstek" station (middle to lower part of boulevard). Wenceslas Square and the surrounding area was an important place of demonstrations during the Velvet Revolution in 1989. There is a big statue of St. Wenceslas riding his horse in the upper part of the boulevard. St. Wenceslas is the patron of Czech lands, so this monument was the focal point of the anticommunist demonstrations. Just few dozen meters down from the monument, at the place where Jan Palach burned himself in 1969 in protest against Soviet occupation of Czechoslovakia, there is a marble plate in memory of the victims of communism. The St. Wenceslas statue is also a popular meeting point; if somebody in Prague wants to meet u koně (near the horse) or pod ocasem (under the horse tail), this place is meant. A notable building is the beautiful Hotel Evropa in Art Nouveau style (1906) in the middle of the boulevard.

listings.name: National Museum
listings.content: Nature and history museum in the upper part of Wenceslas Square. The building was designed by prominent Czech neo-renaissance architect Josef Schulz in the years 1885 - 1891. In the older museum, there is an excellent permanent exhibition of various minerals including gems, as well as other interesting exhibitions including insects, fossils, animal skeletons, and stuffed animals from around the world. One of the best known pieces is a large whale skeleton hanging from the ceiling, quite unusual in a landlocked country. The building is enormous and the architecture very grand, but the exhibitions in themselves need to be fixed up. New museum has exhibitions on communism.
listings.price: Adult 360 Kč, concession 260 Kč, kids under 15 free

listings.name: Dancing House
listings.content: It is the work of the twentieth century American architect Frank Gehry, and is said to be shaped like a man and a woman dancing; hence its former name "Fred and Ginger". Inside you can visit a gallery or go to the rooftop bar and restaurant and enjoy nice views of the river and castle.

listings.name: Botanical Garden of the Charles University
listings.content: Botanical garden of the Charles University with valuable outdoor exhibition and a collection of tropical plants in greenhouses.

listings.name: Vyšehrad
listings.content: Seat of Czech princes for centuries before Prague Castle was built. Site of St. Paul and Peter's Cathedral, and of the famous Vyšehrad cemetery known as 'Slavín', burial grounds of extraordinary Czechs. Don't forget to visit the casemate of Vyšehrad; they are picturesque, and you can see originals of some statues from Charles Bridge. From the ramparts of Vyšehrad, you'll have an excellent view of Prague castle, Vltava, Smíchov (former workers' slum and industrial quarter of town) and Podskalí (area under Vyšehrad, once inhabited almost entirely by raftsmen). If you take a look from southern rampart, you'll see Kavčí hory, headquarters of Czech Television - rather futuristic building from the 1960s. For closer look to Kavčí hory, take metro line C, station "Pražského povstání".

listings.name: Vyšehrad cemetery
listings.content: Established in 1869 on the grounds of Vyšehrad Castle, it is the final resting place of many famous Czechs like artist Alphonse Mucha and writers Jan Neruda and Karel Čapek.

listings.name: Basilica of St Peter and St Paul
listings.content: A neo-Gothic church in Vyšehrad fortress.

listings.name: Velvet Revolution Memorial
listings.content: A simple brass plaque.

listings.name: Jubilee Synagogue
listings.content: Built in 1906, designed in Moorish Revival form with Art Nouveau decoration.

listings.name: Museum of Communism
listings.content: An interesting museum that follows the history of communism in Czech Republic until its fall with the Velvet Revolution. The museum has several interesting communist propaganda artifacts, which are worth a look. Interesting exhibits on how communism changed Czechoslovakia, but skewed toward a particular view of history.
listings.price: Adults 390 Kč, students with ID 310 Kč, seniors 340 Kč

listings.name: Mucha Museum
listings.content: This museum is dedicated to the life and works of Alphonse Mucha, a leading artist in the Art Nouveau movement.
listings.price: Adults 300 Kč, concessions 250 Kč, kids under 10 free

listings.name: Head of Franz Kafka
listings.content: A moving metallic sculpture behind the Quadrio mall.

listings.name: Emauzy monastery
listings.content: Founded in 1347 by Charles IV, Emauzy is a historic Benedictine abbey known for hosting Slavic liturgy. Destroyed by World War II bombing and famously restored in the 1960s with modern white concrete towers, it features original 14th-century Gothic cloisters and frescoes.
listings.price: Adult 90 Kč, concessions 60 Kč, family 150 Kč

listings.name: Máj Národní
listings.content: A former shopping center, multiple floors now covered by arcade games and Marvel/DC-movie-heroes-related showcases. Top floor with city overview freely accessible. On the building facade are placed plane-butterfly art pieces.

listings.name: National Theatre
listings.content: The original National Theatre building. The interior of the building is very decorative, and a sight of its own. Sometimes hosts operas and ballets, but mostly plays in Czech language; English surtitles are often available. Students receive a 50% discount on tickets.

listings.name: Mánes Gallery
listings.content: A renowned functionalist exhibition space built between 1928 and 1930 on the Vltava Riverbank. Designed by Otakar Novotný, it serves as a major venue for modern and contemporary art, managed by the historic Mánes Association of Fine Artists, hosting exhibitions, social events, and offering iconic views near the Dancing House. Opening times and prices can be found on their website and may vary depending on the exhibition.

listings.name: Dietní jídelna
listings.content: Canteen specialising in healthy food. The dishes are presented on a plate which makes it easier to choose. Open M-F 11:00-14:00

listings.name: Wokin
listings.content: Stir-fries. It is possible to order on the app or kiosk and the food usually comes out quick.

listings.name: Bageterie Boulevard
listings.content: Czech fast-food chain that focuses on fresh, gourmet baguettes, soups, salads, and breakfast items.

listings.name: Tian Tian Restaurant
listings.content: Asian restaurant.

listings.name: Zdravé žití U tří růží
listings.content: Vegetarian

listings.name: Střecha
listings.content: Vegan restaurant

listings.name: Plavecká Polévka
listings.content: A bistro

listings.name: Kung Fu Pure Chinese Pasta
listings.content: Dumplings

listings.name: Fresco Vento
listings.content: Italian

listings.name: Jáma³ Garden Pub
listings.content: Good place for burgers. Free wi-fi.

listings.name: Pizzeria Kmotra Kavárna
listings.content: A great, inexpensive pizza place with a relaxed setting.

listings.name: Pivovarský dům Benedikt- restaurace a pivotéka Praha
listings.content: Microbrewery makes everything from a traditional Czech pilsner to beers flavored with sour cherries or banana.

listings.name: Cafe Slavia
listings.content: A coffee tastes even better when accompanied by stunning views of the Vltava and Prague Castle. Cafe Slavia is the perfect place to stop for a coffee or light meal during a day of sightseeing in Castle.

listings.name: Café Louvre
listings.content: Once frequented by Franz Kafka, this cafe is now a popular hotspot for a Prague locals. Their separate dining room offers French cuisine, for those looking for a different option than Czech food.

listings.name: U Kroka
listings.content: Charm restaurant with delicious food and reasonable price. Try the double colored beer!

listings.name: Kantýna
listings.content: Hip, market-style restaurant specializing in different cuts of meat and local side dishes. Most food is by weight: you grab a tray and have the cooks pile on whatever you'd like from their station. There are also items you can order off the menu: the burger and beef tartar are highlights. Outstanding flavors and fresh ingredients.

listings.name: Restaurant Zvonice
listings.content: This romantic restaurant is spread over three levels high up in a Gothic bell tower. If you're lucky, you will get to eat dinner immediately beneath a huge bell.
listings.price: Mains approximately 600 Kč, bottles of wine 800 Kč to 7000 Kč.

listings.name: Triton
listings.content: Upscale restaurant, sea themed, located completely underground. Excellent food in an unusual decor, ideally suited for romantic dinners for two. Not suited for kids. The entrance is somewhat hard to find, ask in the bar on street level for directions.

listings.name: Duplex
listings.content: Situated in Wenceslas Square, this club pays US$5000 rent per day, and consequently charges an outrageous cover fee to teenage tourists who still think that Prague is the "wild" place it was in the early 1990s. This club does a good job of keeping the more pleasant clubs in Prague free from tourists who come for Prague's more disreputable aspects.

listings.name: Lucerna Music Bar
listings.content: Nice, but a little touristy; they play mostly 1980s music (with the accompanying music video on the big screen).

listings.name: U Fleků
listings.content: A restaurant that brews its own fantastic dark, sweet beer. It is the color of Coca-Cola with an alcohol content of 5.5% ABV, but its flavor is not overly strong. The servers will suggest a shot of local herb liqueur, Becherovka, but it won't be free. The atmosphere of this pub gets very rowdy as it is loaded with tourists from all over and bands play regularly. It's a lot of fun with a group.
listings.price: U Fleků 13° 99 Kč and spirits around 79 Kč

listings.name: Vinarna U Sudu
listings.content: An incredible wine bar that doesn't look like much from the front, but if you look inside and go in the way back you'll find a huge underground maze of different areas each with their own unique music and vibe. Also nearby is the crossing point for all night trams.

listings.name: Bike 7
listings.content: In the evening, bars in port holes along the riverwalk open up. (Also a few on barges.) Popular with locals, they have lots of outdoor tables. Great place to people watch, and also see night fall over the castle on the hill.

listings.name: Best Prague Hotel House
listings.content: Apartments where can sleep up to four people with living room, bathroom and kitchen from 2450 Kč per night. Higher rates apply during peak season and for more than 2 guests.

listings.name: Hotel Elite
listings.content: Luxury 4-star hotel on the edge of Old Town and New Town. 78 rooms containing pieces of original antique furniture, A/C, private bathroom, IDD, pay TV, satellite, free WiFi, safety deposit box and a minibar, wellness, hotel garages.

listings.name: Hotel Atlantic
listings.content: A 3-star hotel located in the City Center on walking distance from all major historical sites. It offers 62 spacious, comfortable rooms, of which 3 have access for disabled people. Rooms are fitted with shower, WC, satellite TV, direct-dial (IDD) telephone, wifi and safety deposit box.

listings.name: Hotel Best Western Meteor Plaza
listings.content: 4-star hotel just outside the Old Town gate, within walking distance of much of the city centre. Amenities include air conditioning, shower and/or bath, WC, hair dryer, satellite/pay TV, IDD telephone, personal safe, coffee/tea maker, and mini-bar. Rate includes breakfast and wireless Internet access.

listings.name: Miss Sophie's
listings.content: This designer boutique hotel/hostel is the perfect destination for a quiet getaway in the heart of Prague's New Town. Miss Sophie's offers private hotel rooms, apartments, and shared rooms. Gourmet breakfast is prepared and served daily in brick cellar basement.
listings.price: Prices start at 420 Kč for a shared room and 1,630 Kč for a private room.

listings.name: Mosaic House
listings.content: A unique blend of 4-star hotel and hostel. Downstairs, the restaurant and bar have a wide variety of local and international food and drink options. It's a blend of style, ecofriendly features, fun, and culture for all ages. Prices range from 250 Kč for a shared room and 1,400 Kč for a private double. Modern, eco-friendly, and centrally located. From shared rooms to private rooms with terraces, all are beautifully designed with cozy linens, gorgeous bathrooms, modern amenities. Also on premises is Belushi's Bar and Restaurant , which offers great food and drinks and live entertainment. Breakfast is served from 07:00 through 11:30, with omelettes and scrambled eggs, pancakes and fresh fruits, fresh breads from their local bakery, coffee and tea. Lunch, dinner, late night eats, and everything in between served until 23:00. You can select from burgers and sandwich options galore, tasty salads, filling appetizers and specialty desserts menu.

listings.name: Dahlia Inn
listings.content: Family-run accommodation.

listings.name: Palace Hotel
listings.content: Luxury five-star hotel just off Wenceslas Square.

listings.name: 987 Prague Hotel
listings.content: For €1 more get free phone calls to Europe. Free internet.

listings.name: Deminka Palace Hotel
listings.content: Located in Prague city center, near the National Museum.

listings.name: Hotel Merlin
listings.content: Three-star accommodation in the center of Prague on the banks of the Vltava River, next to Dancing House near the metro station Karlovo náměstí

listings.name: Apartments Emma
listings.content: Apartments from two to four people to rent near Vysehrad castle. Kitchen, internet and no curfew. The host is very helpful for information about public transport, attractions and night life.
listings.price: From 800 Kč for 2-person studio during low season. Rates are higher at peak times

listings.name: Botel Racek
listings.content: A hotel boat on the Vltava river offering rooms and suites, all with private bathroom, TV and phone. There's a Czech restaurant on board and you can enjoy drinks on the deck or in the bar. Botel Racek is ten minutes away from the city centre by tram and has private parking available. Singles, doubles, triples and quads. Prices vary depending on season, there are last minute offers.

listings.name: Easy Housing
listings.content: Hostel.

listings.name: Old Town Square
listings.content: The center of the eventful history of Prague. The Gothic, Renaissance and Baroque buildings were preserved here. The Historical Centre, including most of the city’s major sites, became a UNESCO-listed site in 1992.

listings.name: Týn Church
listings.content: A very striking pure Gothic church on the outside, with a beautiful Baroque interior. The interior is free to visit with a suggested donation, but everyone except for worshippers at Mass must stay in the entryway area and no photos are allowed. You still have a very good view of most of the details of the interior from behind the rope, however, and it's well worth it for you to enter. Entry is via a building on Old Town Square.

listings.name: Storch Building
listings.content: Covered in murals.

listings.name: Jan Hus Memorial
listings.content: That striking man standing atop a patina-green metal mountain in the center of Old Town Square is not Jesus, though he resembles him. It's Jan Hus, the great Czech religious reformer whose Hussite movement caused as much, if not more, friction within the Christian community than Martin Luther. The statue was erected on the 500th anniversary of his death (6 July 1915). Hus preached in the Bethlehem Church in Old Town. He believed in Bibles written in the worshiper's language, in the importance of faith instead of a clergyman's intermediation with God - in other words, concepts which threatened the status quo. He was summoned to the Church's Council of Constance in Switzerland by representatives of the Emperor, and given a letter of safe conduct to get there and back. Like every member of the Habsburg family, before and after him, the Emperor was Catholic. After Hus refused to repent for his so-called sins and come back into the Church, he was burned at the stake, despite the promise of the Emperor.

listings.name: Astronomical Clock
listings.content: The Astronomical Clock located on a side tower of the Old Town Hall (reasonably enough, on Old Town Square) is easy to find—just wait until a few minutes before the hour and look for a large group of tourists standing around waiting for something to happen! Still, Orloj is one of the most popular gathering places in Prague. The closer you are to the astronomical clock, the more astronomical the prices in restaurants and stores.Built in 1410 and thought of as an example of 15th century high-tech device, projected with the participation of maths and astronomy professors at Prague University. The main dial is in principle a mechanical astrolabe, showing not only the current time, but also the placement of the sun and moon in the Zodiac, phases of the moon, the times of sunrise and sunset, length of astronomical night, the time in old Bohemian hours, in unequal hours and other data. From gathering crowds, hardly anybody understands all data astronomical dial displays.Then there is a slow-moving 12-month calendar with incredibly delicate, small figure paintings by 19th century Czech painter Josef Manes. Every day on the hour, the upper, glockenspiel-style section of the clock performs the same scene: Death waves an hourglass, the 12 apostles shuffle past small windows, and a rooster crows. After the hour strikes, a Turk wags his head.Long after the Turks had ceased to be a threat in Central Europe, their use as an allegorical figure in genre paintings and other art continued. The Czechs often sided with the Hungarians in various battles against increasing imperial power as exercised by the ruling Habsburg family over their dominions, and though the Turks never occupied Prague as they did Budapest, both countries' artists used "the Turk" (a dark-complected figure, usually wearing a turban) to represent the dangers of the world, and especially threats to Christianity. In the astronomical clock, the Turk is meant to be the stranger.There is a legend about the clock that states the original master builder of its interior clockworks was blinded by the King who commissioned it after the work was completed so the mechanic could never build such a wonderful clock for someone else. In vengeance, the master builder committed suicide by throwing himself into the gears of the clock, which took nearly a century to be repaired. Pickpocketing is common in this location.

listings.name: Municipal House
listings.content: Nám. Republiky 5. The Obecní dům was built near the Powder Tower (a storage place for gunpowder and a major trade route entry into the city) on a site called King's Court where once a royal residence stood. In 1901, the Prague Civic Society made a proposal to city authorities to build a center for official and social Czech events. As happened so many other times in recent Prague history, the Czechs were trying to balance the grand buildings erected by the German-speaking community of Prague with suitable edifices of their own. The "German House" (now co-opted and renamed Slovanský dům, or Slavic House, on Na Příkopě street) and a German casino were enough to make the Czechs want a place of their own. Unless you have tickets to an event, the rooms other than the foyer can only be seen on a guided tour (separate tours in Czech and English, information booklets available in other world languages).

listings.name: Prague City Gallery
listings.content: A museum of modern Czech arts divided between several sites most of which are in the old town. Its main building is the House of the Golden Ring at the Old Town Square featuring 20th century Czech art in a beautiful medieval edifice. 19th century Czech art is exhibited at the Troja Castle.
listings.image: Praha Old Town sq U zvonu CIMG0089.JPG

listings.name: Speculum Alchemiae
listings.content: A museum dedicated to the mysteries of alchemy, housed in a classified building dated from 980 AD in the center of the Jewish district, one of the only authentic buildings preserved after the massive redevelopment of the Old Town's Jewish Quarter during the 19th century. Only guided tours available in English or Czech. Tours include a history of alchemy, the role of the Kings in the alchemical development of Prague, the search for various elixirs and the relation with golems, and a tour through the laboratories in the underground catacombs under the city, dating from the 16th century renaissance period. Duration: 30 - 40 minutes. The catacombs are fairly cold even in summer, so warm clothing is recommended.

listings.name: Convent of Saint Agnes
listings.content: The Anezsky klaster is the first Early Gothic building in Prague (founded 1234) - something notable in a city filled with amazingly well-preserved examples of Gothic architecture such as St Vitus, the Charles Bridge and the Powder Tower. Over the years the complex's convent, chapels and several churches deteriorated and in some cases, were completely destroyed. After Habsburg emperor Josef II's religious reforms, the convent was shut down in 1782 and converted into lodgings for the poor. St Anežka, (Sv. Anežka česká) who is pictured on the pink 50 Kč banknote, is the patron saint of Bohemia and founder of the convent complex. She was a daughter of the ruling Premyslid family, but no wallflower in terms of her activism, intelligence and energy. St Francis of Assisi, after whom one of the churches in the complex is named, founded his religious order in 1209 without the sort of financial backing earlier orders had enjoyed. As communism was crumbling, the remaining religious leadership, decimated over years by Communism's anti-religious influence, lobbied the Vatican to finally declare Anežka a saint. This happened 12 November 1989, though Anežka's niece Elizabeth had started the process in 1328! Today, the convent is used to house part of the Czech National Gallery's collection.
listings.price: Admission: Full: 220 Kč, Reduced: 120 Kč, Family: 150 Kč
listings.image: Praha, Štefánikův most, Anežský klášter small.jpg

listings.name: Museum of Czech Cubism
listings.content: The Museum of Czech Cubism in the renovated House of the Black Madonna exhibits furniture suites, individual pieces, accessory furnishings and objects made of ceramic, glass and metals. It offers an overview of the foremost creative achievements of Czech Cubism’s key exponents. This unique Cubist building, designed by Josef Gočár, was built in 1911–1912.
listings.price: Adult 150 Kč, senior or student 80 Kč (July 2020)

listings.name: Museum of Decorative Arts
listings.content: This 17th century palazzo-style building houses examples of historical and contemporary crafts, as well as applied arts and design.
listings.image: Building of Museum of Decorative Arts in Prague.jpg

listings.name: Church of the Holy Spirit
listings.content: Baroque church

listings.name: Pariska Street
listings.content: Tree lined street with number of historic buildings, exclusive shopping and upmarket restaurants and hotels.

listings.name: Rudolfinum
listings.content: Neo-Renaissance auditorium, home of the Czech Philharmonic Orchestra. A statue of Antonin Dvořak is in the park in front of the building, whose front façade is being renovated as of August 2026.

listings.name: Jaroslav Fragner Gallery
listings.content: Contemporary architecture. You can find here profiles of influential people and groups, retrospective exhibitions, thematic exhibitions, recent movement in architecture. Gallery provides lectures, seminars and publishing, regarding central Prague. The JFG is a centre for architects, professional and general public, students of architecture and construction companies.

listings.name: Sex Machines Museum
listings.content: Humorous presentation of historic and present day sex toys and related installations. A visit takes about 60 to 90 minutes, and offers an initiation in the world of domestic and commercial pleasure engineering. No entry for persons under 18; not suitable for physically disabled people, due to the very steep stairs.

listings.name: Lego Museum
listings.content: A small museum dedicated to Lego bricks and their creations. Don't expect a history of the bricks, the museum is entirely focused on Lego constructions applied to the Czech context, with many monuments of Prague replicated as scale models in Lego. Most of the models on display are standard sets however, so the museum will be only worth its entrance fee for die hard Lego fans.

listings.name: Powder Tower
listings.content: One of the original city gates, which separates the Old Town from the New Town. The gate was used to store gunpowder in the 17th century, hence the name Powder Tower or Powder Gate.
listings.image: Prague 07-2016 Powder Tower from Republic Square.jpg

listings.name: Jewish Museum
listings.content: This is not a single site but consists of four synagogues, the Old Jewish Cemetery and the Memorial Hall - entrance to all being covered by a single ticket. A combined ticket that includes the Old-New Synagogue can be obtained at a considerable extra cost but the interest of the building justifies it.

listings.name: Maisel Synagogue
listings.content: One of the historical monuments of the former Prague Jewish Ghetto. Nowadays the synagogue belongs to the Jewish Community of Prague and is administered by the Jewish Museum in Prague as a part of its expositions.

listings.name: Spanish Synagogue
listings.content: The Spanish Synagogue, so-called because Sephardic Jews expelled from Spain at the end of the 15th century built a previous synagogue on this site, is a wild combination of neo-Renaissance and Moorish-Spain style. Think the Alhambra crossed with a Victorian wallpaper store, with some Islamic geometric and floral flourishes thrown in for good measure. The predominant color is red, which lends a regal aura to the interior, but there are also multiple shades of green and blue. The background behind the altar is blue covered with gold stars, visually implying the intercession of the deity in the holy space of the building, drawing one's eyes upward to the vast ceiling.

listings.name: Pinkas Synagogue
listings.content: Inside the front door of the Pinkas Synagogue, inscribed in tiny red and black letters on almost every square inch of wallspace are the names of 77,297 Jews who were killed in the war. This visual representation humanizes such a number, attaching names to the statistics. In larger type at the front of the synagogue are the names of the concentration camps in which they perished: Dachau, Mauthausen, Oswiecim (Auschwitz) and others. The second floor houses a moving exhibit of children's art which is smaller than the original exhibit at Terezin but no less sad.

listings.name: Old Jewish Cemetery
listings.content: On the left wall before the entrance is a plaque detailing conservation efforts (which cost 1 million crowns per year). Over 20,000 people are buried in about twelve layers of graves, stacked to save space. Avigdor Kara is the earliest known person buried here - he was a poet who lived to tell about the 1389 pogrom. The reddish, grey and black tombstones are tilted at crazy angles, some covered with moss, some newly cleaned. Walking along the path that winds around the perimeter, Rabbi Loew's tombstone is about halfway through. It has a lion on it and a plaque on the wall across from it. Loew is known as the father of the Golem legend in Prague.

listings.name: Klausen Synagogue
listings.content: The Klausen Synagogue is nowadays the largest synagogue in the former Prague Jewish ghetto and also a single example of an early Baroque synagogue in the area.

listings.name: Ceremonial Hall
listings.content: The last service to the deceased members of the Prague Jewish Community was held here.
listings.image: Jewish Ceremonial Hall Prague Czech Rep.jpg

listings.name: Old-New Synagogue
listings.content: The name sounds strange for a building from the 13th century but it was called 'New' to distinguish it from an even older synagogue. This was replaced by the Spanish Synagogue in the 17th century, when the Old-New Synagogue acquired its current name. It is rumoured to be the resting place of the famed Prague Golem.

listings.name: Jewish Town Hall
listings.content: Renaissance-style building

listings.name: Stavovské divadlo
listings.content: Oldest theatre building still standing in the city. Mozart's opera Don Giovanni was premiered here, with Mozart personally conducting, and Don Giovanni is still often in the repertoire, as are other operas, plays and ballets.

listings.name: Thrill Park Prague
listings.content: A haunted house with actors and VR zombie shooting.

listings.name: FunCity Prague Arcade
listings.content: Game mashines

listings.name: City Game Prague
listings.content: Interactive outdoor games and quizzes guided simply via WhatsApp messenger chat.

listings.name: Hacker's Nest
listings.content: Interactive co-op puzzle game requiring players to work together to save the world from destruction. Players solve puzzles and uncover mysteries in a race against time, attempting to defeat the doomsday plan from an Anonymous hacker. Minimum 2 players. No knowledge of hacker culture required, but minimal technical skills are helpful. Play time is 60 minutes. It is a relatively difficult game, not recommended for new players.

listings.name: Grand Cafe Orient
listings.content: Coffee, tea, cakes and sandwiches with free wi-fi between Namesti Republiky and the Old Town Square.
listings.address: Dům u Černé Matky Boží, Ovocny trh 19

listings.name: La Casa Blu
listings.content: Spanish/Mexican food at good prices, close to Dlouha Trida tram stop. Free wi-fi internet. Service can be slow.

listings.name: Lokál
listings.content: A new member to famous Ambi restaurants group, this is the place, where traditional and modern blend together. While evoking Czech pubs from times years ago, everything is brand new. Beer (35 Kč) and food (100 - 200 Kč) is very good. Large non-smoking section in the back.

listings.name: Restaurace Konvikt
listings.content: Authentic local pub and restaurant

listings.name: Dinitz Kosher Restaurant
listings.content: Middle Eastern specials, in this Israeli restaurant offering Glatt kosher meals. The highlight is the Famous Sampler Menu, which consists of many tapas-style plates & mixed grilled meat on skewers.

listings.name: V Kolkovně
listings.content: Offers a combination of the tradition and uniqueness of the Pilsner Urquell brand and traditional Czech cuisine fused with modern gastronomy (French, German and International influences).

listings.name: Kafka snob food
listings.content: Good breakfast, nice place to sit at a street table with a coffee. Service can range from very good to poor depending who is working that day.

listings.name: Indian Jewel
listings.content: Very good Indian restaurant

listings.name: Kavárna Obecní dům
listings.content: Good selection of food in an interesting setting.

listings.name: Bakeshop
listings.content: A cafe with a large selection of warm drinks and cakes. Finding seating is not guaranteed during the busiest hours of the day, so check for seating before ordering unless you're planning to eat underway.

listings.name: Five Rivers
listings.content: Family friendly Indian restaurant, bar, cafe. Menu includes vegetarian and non vegetarian starter, main course and dessert. Free Wi-Fi, historical exhibit, no selfie ban.

listings.name: Maitrea
listings.content: Vegetarian restaurant with many vegan options. Wide range of food including both local and more international dishes.

listings.name: Ambiante Pizza Nuova
listings.content: An upscale place which does a very accurate rendition of Neapolitan pizza, but whose real selling point is the amazing play area for small and smallish kids.

listings.name: Field
listings.content: Michelin-starred fine-dining restaurant led by chef Radek Kašpárek. It focuses on modern European cuisine built around seasonal, locally sourced Czech ingredients.

listings.name: La Dégustation Bohême Bourgeoise
listings.content: Often voted as the best Czech restaurant, with price matching the quality. But if you have the cash, it's supposed to be a culinary experience as no other. Menu from 2200 Kč to over 4000 Kč with wine included. One of two restaurants in Prague with a Michelin star.

listings.name: Marina Ristorante
listings.content: Italian restaurant on a boat providing views across to lower town and the castle.

listings.name: Robotic Bar
listings.content: Cocktails from 140 Kč (May 2022) mixed by robots

listings.name: Ice Pub
listings.content: Drinks served in an ice-cold environment. You get a winter jacket there.

listings.name: AghaRTA Jazz Centrum
listings.content: AghaRTA is another well known jazz club, and organizer of the Prague Jazz Festival.

listings.name: Al Capone's Cocktail Bar
listings.content: Al Capone's is a small and family-like bar, located in the very centre, with acceptable prices.
listings.price: Beer 25 Kč-70 Kč, cocktails 45 Kč-80 Kč

listings.name: Chateau Rouge
listings.content: Three-floor club in the old town. Plenty of tourists, including Americans and pub crawl groups, to be found any night of the week.

listings.name: Karlovy lázně
listings.content: This self-styled "biggest music club in Central Europe" is right next to Charles Bridge, with 5 floors of clubs each featuring a different style of music. It is frequented by Czech teenagers and German high school students. There are security guards at the door who search entering patrons. It is more often than not incredibly dirty and filled with very young males.

listings.name: Music Club Zlatý Strom
listings.content: Lively half dance club, half go-go club. Watch out for the bucket mojito cocktails for 599Kč!

listings.name: U Zlatého Tygra
listings.content: If you aren't easily scared off by smoke so thick you can touch and mean-looking Czechs that look like they would rather shake you than share a table, then this place is a must-stop. It is almost always crowded to standing capacity but if you stop by just before closing during the week, you can usually grab a table next to a local or knowledgeable expat and have some great Pilsner Urquell for 34 Kč a half liter, a price that is almost charitably low for the city center. There's also a simple menu of snacks and mains for around 35 Kč-90 Kč. Check the picture on the wall- that's President Bill Clinton drinking here. Favored hangout of the late Czech author Bohumil Hrabal, whose bronze bust stands watch over the heads of patrons.

listings.name: Restaurant Franze Kafky
listings.content: Pleasant place to sit with a drink and people watch in the evening when the establishments on the old town square insist on food only customers.

listings.name: Hotel U Tri Bubnu
listings.content: Small 3-star hotel with unique rooms.

listings.name: Four Seasons Hotel Prague
listings.content: On the river very close to the Charles Bridge. The Four Seasons is best known for having lowered the wall in front that protected it from the flood. But when dry it's as close as you get on the right bank to everything in Prague.
listings.price: Bed and breakfast for 2 people is approximately €250, advance purchase packages are available for as low as €195 per night

listings.name: Hilton Prague Old Town
listings.content: The hotel has 303 rooms, a restaurant on site, a wellness center with fitness equipment and a swimming pool. Room service is available.

listings.name: Hotel Cerny Slon
listings.content: Small, family run 4-star hotel a few meters from the Old Town Square. Rooms have private bathroom, satellite TV, IDD telephone, WiFi and safety deposit boxes.

listings.name: Fairmont Golden Prague Hotel
listings.content: One of the older Western hotels in Prague. Closed for renovation until late 2024, when it is planned to open as a 297 room 5* hotel.

listings.name: Brewery Hotel - U Medvídků
listings.content: On the site of an old brewery that is now a Czech Budweiser (Budvar) restaurant, the pension building houses a brewing museum and shop. It is also connected to a smaller bar that is open until 03:00. The rooms are clean and atmospheric. Ask for a room at the very top (#43 is a good pick) to avoid street/restaurant noise. Rates are seasonal but start from around 1550 Kč/2300 Kč/3100 Kč per night for singles/doubles/triples off peak. Add an extra 10% if you want one of the beautifully restored historical rooms.

listings.name: The U Prince
listings.content: Comfortable beds and beautiful marble bathrooms. The terrace bar has a view of the city and Old Town Square.

listings.name: Clarion Hotel Prague Old Town
listings.content: Near Old Town Square Modern equipment and services in a historic building dating back to 1930. Renovated rooms have internet, free WiFi in common areas.

listings.name: Buddha-Bar Hotel Prague
listings.content: Vibrant music and oriental aromas in the historic city centre of Prague.

listings.name: Hotel Melantrich
listings.content: Comfortably equipped fully en-suite rooms.

listings.name: Grand Hotel Praha
listings.content: Luxury hotel in a historical building. Rooms with a view of the Apostolic Clock and the Old Town Square.

listings.name: Hotel Rott
listings.content: Comfortable accommodation in rooms styled in the late 19th century style, with modern amenities.

listings.name: Hotel Paris
listings.content: 86 room art nouveau hotel built in 1905.

listings.name: Žižkov Television Tower
listings.content: Rumoured to have been intended by the communists to jam western radio signals (but not completed until 1992), the most hideous building in Prague offers spectacular views of the city. The cafe at the top is a great place to grab a coffee and enjoy the view. Look for the giant metallic alien babies added to the outside of tower, which have helped to soften critiques of the tower's harsh architecture.
listings.price: Admission to the observation deck is 350 Kč for adults (there is no fee for restaurants or to access the park at ground level)

listings.name: National Memorial on the Vítkov Hill
listings.content: "Žižkov Monument", located at the top of Vítkov Hill. This immense equestrian statue was erected in 1950 to commemorate the Czech national hero Jan Žižka, who fought his most famous battle on this site and later had the hill and the neighbouring city renamed after himself. The scale of the monument is impressive enough, but the views of Žižkov (and the rest of Prague) from the top of the hill really make the climb worthwhile.

listings.name: Military Museum
listings.content: Showcases the uniforms, weapons, artifacts, and maps relating to the Czechoslovak armed forces during World Wars I and II. Interactive exhibitions on the World Wars from the Czechoslovakian perspective. Free entrance. Not recommended for young children due to shocking content (war crimes among others).

listings.name: Church of the Most Sacred Heart of Our Lord
listings.content: Probably the most unusual and monumental modern church, it dominates the big Jiřího z Poděbard Square. Among other things, the biggest tower clock of the country is located here. Built between 1928 and 1932 and designed by the Slovene architect Jože Plečnik. Candidate to get on UNESCO list. For modern architecture lovers, this is definitely a must! After visiting the church, you can buy something at the popular farmer's market nearby.

listings.name: New Jewish Cemetery
listings.content: Franz Kafka's grave is signposted around 100m along the path to your right from the entrance. Men should cover their heads. The cemetery is closed on Saturdays.

listings.name: Olšany Cemetery
listings.content: After day in a busy city, a walk through the vast and calm Olšany Cemetery is a great idea! It is the largest graveyard in Prague, remarkable for its many art nouveau monuments. The cemetery has a calm and mysterious atmosphere, some parts of it are very old. Famous people such as Jan Palach (a student who set himself on fire in protest against apathy of people during communism), Klement Gottwald (the first communist president of Czechoslovakia), 19th-century writer Karel Havlíček Borovský, actors Rudolf Hrušínský and Jan Werich and many others are buried here.

listings.name: Old Olšany Jewish Cemetery
listings.content: Used since the late 18th century, when the well-known Old Jewish Cemetery in Old Town ceased to be used. One century later, the bigger New Cemetery was built (see above). Located right under the Žižkov TV Tower, more than half of the cemetery was destroyed.

listings.name: Prague Zoo
listings.content: Founded in 1931, it is well known for its significant contribution to saving many species, most notably the Przewalski horse. In 2008 Forbes Traveler Magazine listed Prague Zoo as the 7th best in the world. The zoo occupies 45 hectares (111 acres) and houses over 5000 animals that represent 674 species from all around the world (as of December 31, 2008). There is also a chairlift in the zoo.

listings.name: Prague Botanical Garden
listings.content: Open air exhibitions including the historical vineyard of St. Claire and the Japanese garden. Tropical greenhouse Fata morgana. Each year in spring there is an exhibition of living butterflies.

listings.name: Troja Palace
listings.content: Baroque chateau with garden and art exhibitions. The Prague City Gallery's collection of 19th-century Czech art is exhibited here.

listings.name: Intelligence Bridge
listings.content: A majestic railway bridge built in the 1950s, the longest ferroconcrete railway bridge in Europe. It was built by forced labour of members of the intelligentsia, who were transferred to manual professions by rule of communist government. As a monument to the stupidity of the communist rulers, only a single rail was laid on the two-rail bridge, because the second rail didn't fit into the tunnel on one bank. The bridge remains in service to this day and is used mainly for freight trains.

listings.name: Kbely Aviation Museum
listings.content: Part of the Military Museum, opened in the 1960s on the grounds of former military airfield. One of the largest museums of this type in Europe, has 275 aircraft, of which around 100 are displayed.

listings.name: Invalidovna
listings.content: It may seem like a big chateau, but Invalidovna was a baroque dormitory in operation from 1737 for war invalids, built by famous architect Kilián Ignác Dientzenhofer. It was damaged during the 2002 floods and only the front facade has been reconstructed since. In front of the building there is a very nice and tidy park.

listings.name: Podolí Waterworks Building
listings.content: This monumental building from the late 1920s might look like a parliament building or at least a town hall, but it's just a waterworks. Located by the Vltava river, the industrial building was built in the neoclassical style by architect Antonín Engel. You can visit the museum of Prague water supply there.

listings.name: St. Wenceslas Church
listings.content: Big functionalist church by famous architect Josef Gočár in Vršovice.

listings.name: Havlíčkovy sady
listings.content: A quiet little park with an interesting artificial cave building, "Grotta". A good relaxing place near the city center.

listings.name: Libeň Gas Reservoir
listings.content: A large metal ball which used to serve as a gas canister. You can not get inside, but it is still interesting to see it from the outside.

listings.name: World of Jellyfish
listings.content: A jellyfish exposition accompanied with audio-visual effects, with more than 10,000 jellyfish specimens and 38 aquariums (including one of the biggest sphere-shaped aquariums of the world).

listings.name: Státní opera
listings.content: This historic building of the former German Theatre now serves as the State Opera, hosting mainly operas and ballets.

listings.name: Forum Karlín
listings.content: Multifunctional auditorium for 3,000 people where different cultural events take place.

listings.name: Palác Akropolis
listings.content: An alternative club that often hosts international rock acts.

listings.name: Podolí Swimming Stadion
listings.content: Old, famous and big swimming areal including three big pools (one inside and two outside), fitness, sauna and massages

listings.name: Unikovehryvpraze.cz
listings.content: Escape games. You are ushered into the room, the door slams behind you and the clock starts.

listings.name: Kino Aero
listings.content: Small art-house style cinema. Film festivals. Many English language films shown with Czech subtitles.

listings.name: Pizzeria Aria
listings.content: A pizzeria on walking distance from the bus station, with great value for those who like Italian food. Pasta dishes for around 200 Kč. They also serve Italian and local desserts such as tiramisu and medovnik. A very basic establishment for a quick lunch or dinner. Suitable for kids.

listings.name: U Houdků
listings.content: Traditional (and inexpensive) Czech Restaurant with beer garden in summer. Lunchtime specials are particularly good value.

listings.name: Pho Vietnam
listings.content: Authentic Vietnamese bistro, one of the best in Prague.

listings.name: BarFood
listings.content: Wisconsin-themed American diner serving burgers, sandwiches and chicken wings

listings.name: Žižkovská štrúdlárna
listings.content: Czech cuisine. Home-baked apple strudel. Locally run, so there may be a language barrier.

listings.name: Lokál Hamburk
listings.content: Part of famous Ambi restaurant group.

listings.name: Highland Steak House
listings.content: Steaks and burgers.

listings.name: Plzeňka Olše
listings.content: Czech. Well known for its unpasteurized Pilsner beer. Menu in Czech and English.

listings.name: Spice India
listings.content: Indian and Bangladeshi cuisine. Take-away available. Lunch menu from 150 Kč.

listings.name: Taverna Olympos
listings.content: Greek cuisine

listings.name: Indian Restaurant Pind Prague
listings.content: Indian cuisine, possible to sit outside.

listings.name: U Bohouše
listings.content: Mostly Czech cuisine.

listings.name: Dish Belgická
listings.content: Home-made burgers and chips.

listings.name: Third Coast Pizza
listings.content: Highly filling Detroit-style deep dish pizza joint

listings.name: Pub a Bar Na Plech
listings.content: Czech restaurant with a few vegetarian options.

listings.name: Restaurace u Agamy
listings.content: Restaurant with many gluten-free and dairy-free options, including gluten-free beer

listings.name: Cà Phê Cổ - Prague
listings.content: Vietnamese restaurant.

listings.name: Bruxx
listings.content: Belgian. Seafood and beer (dozens of kinds).

listings.name: Oblaca
listings.content: Award-winning fine dining restaurant on the lower deck of the Žižkov TV tower with spectacular views over the city.

listings.name: Restaurace Chateau St. Havel
listings.content: Located in a renovated neo-Gothic chateau the restaurant offers high-end Czech and European cuisine. Led by renowned TV chef Ondřej Slanina, it provides a romantic, tranquil atmosphere with a terrace overlooking a park.

listings.name: Palác Akropolis
listings.content: An alternative club that often hosts international rock acts.

listings.name: U Sadu
listings.content: Open until 04:00; kitchen also open late, but dependent on customers as to how late.

listings.name: U Vystřelenýho oka
listings.content: Famous Žižkov pub serving Pilsner and Gambrinus on tap. Unusual artwork depicting the Battle of Vítkov Hill. Serves bar food (fried cheese, goulash, sausage). Staff speaks mainly Czech but an English menu is available.

listings.name: Tiki Taky
listings.content: Tiki bar. Specializes in cocktails. Staff speaks Czech and English.

listings.name: Bukowski's Bar
listings.content: Cocktails.

listings.name: Kaaba Café
listings.content: small café, friendly atmosphere

listings.name: Vinohradský pivovar
listings.content: Brewery with restaurant renewed in 2013. Interior of restaurant is very simple and modern.

listings.name: mamacoffe
listings.content: Fair trade café, one of four mamacofee cafés in Prague.

listings.name: U Posledního soudu
listings.content: Small but great and inexpensive wine bar serving Czech wines and wines from neighboring countries.

listings.name: Maleše Microbrewery
listings.content: A nice new brewery in Malešice district.

listings.name: El Mágico
listings.content: A popular club in university campus (thus popular especially among local students).

listings.name: Shadow Cafe
listings.content: A nice rooftop bar near Křížikova metro station. Come early (18:00) on Friday or there will not be a place for you.

listings.name: Bar Milá tchýně
listings.content: A nice bar in Vršovice district, a lot of people on Fridays

listings.name: Café V Lese
listings.content: Café with a gallery and music club, run by famous Czech activist Ondřej Kobza.

listings.name: Kolčavka Brewery
listings.content: A nice small brewery in Libeň district

listings.name: Czech Inn
listings.content: With its chic-modern design, Czech Inn offers a wide variety in accommodation from shared rooms, private double rooms, and apartments. Breakfast buffet served daily, with a trendy bar to try your favorite Czech beers and cocktails. Prices from 275 Kč for a shared room and 1,250 Kč for a private double room.

listings.name: Hostel Elf
listings.content: Husitska 11, Žižkov. Smokey common area, free internet and wacky rooms. Breakfast and free tea and coffee all day are included. Dorms, doubles, triples, privates with bathroom or without. There are four (or more) different seasons with different prices. In low season fifth night free.

listings.name: Clown and Bard Hostel
listings.content: With a lively vibe and a bar in the basement there's always something going on at the hostel too, though it's not the cleanest or newest in town. Free breakfast and internet is available for all guests and rooms in the very large dorm start at 300 Kč. For those who want a little privacy, five-bed dorms, six-bed privates and doubles are available for 380 Kč, 400 Kč and 500 Kč respectively.

listings.name: Guesthouse Chlumova
listings.content: Mid-priced guesthouse located 1 block from the Lipanska (tram 9) tram stop. Private rooms, some with a private bathroom and kitchenette. Staff speaks Czech, English, Spanish and Russian.

listings.name: Hotel Claris
listings.content: All of the 24 rooms are equipped with shower/bath, WC, hair dryer, sat TV, IDD telephone with voice mail, safe and free Wi-Fi.

listings.name: Hotel Anna
listings.content: Each of the 22 rooms is equipped with shower & WC, hair dryer, IDD telephone, satellite TV and a safety deposit box.

listings.name: Clarion Congress Hotel Prague
listings.content: 4-star hotel connected to the Fenix shopping gallery and close to O2 Arena. 559 modernly and appealingly furnished standard and executive rooms. Wireless internet in public areas and wired internet in the rooms. Spa and fitness facilities are available in the building at an additional cost.

listings.name: Hilton Prague
listings.content: Large modern hotel right on the bank of the Vltava close to the Old Town. Double rooms range from €155 per night for a simple guest room to €215 for an executive suite.

places.blurb: The Great Strahov Stadium is a stadium in the Strahov district of Prague, Czech Republic.

places.title: Vyšehrad

places.title: Staropramen Brewery

places.title: Wenceslas Square

places.title: Žižkov Television Tower
places.blurb: The Žižkov Television Tower is a transmitter tower built in Prague between 1985 and 1992.

places.title: Old New Synagogue
places.blurb: The Old New Synagogue, also called the Altneuschul, is an Orthodox Jewish congregation and synagogue, located in Josefov, Prague, in the Czech Republic.

places.title: Petřín Lookout Tower
places.blurb: The Petřín Lookout Tower is a steel-framework tower 63.5 metres tall on Petřín Hill in Prague, built in 1891.

places.title: U Fleků
places.blurb: U Fleků is a pub and microbrewery in Prague, Czech Republic.

places.title: New Town, Prague

places.title: National Museum
places.blurb: The National Museum is a public museum dedicated to natural scientific and historical collections of the Czech Republic, its history, culture and people, among others.

places.title: Letná

places.title: Old Town Square

places.title: Nusle Bridge

places.title: Wallenstein Palace
places.blurb: Waldstein Palace is a Baroque palace in Malá Strana, Prague, that served as a residence for Imperial Generalissimo Albrecht von Waldstein and now houses the Senate of the Czech Republic.

places.title: National Technical Museum
places.blurb: The National Technical Museum in Prague is the largest institution dedicated to preserving information and artifacts related to the history of technology in the Czech Republic.

places.title: Letná Park
places.blurb: Letná Park is a park in Prague, Czech Republic.

places.title: Stalin Monument
places.blurb: Stalin's Monument was a 15.5 m granite statue honoring Joseph Stalin in Prague, Czechoslovakia.
